On Keeping Notebooks

There is something quietly heroic about a blank notebook. It asks nothing of you, yet promises everything: a place where half-formed thoughts can survive long enough to become real ideas. Most of our mental life evaporates—a dream forgotten by breakfast, a perfect sentence composed in the shower and lost by the towel. The notebook is a small act of rebellion against that constant erosion.

I think about the people who filled theirs obsessively. Darwin recording the plumage of birds he'd never fully understand. Da Vinci sketching water spirals beside grocery lists. Somewhere, an anonymous medieval monk doodled cats in the margins of manuscripts he was copying, and those doodles outlived nearly everything else from his century. We remember him, faintly, because he couldn't resist drawing a cat.

A notebook doesn't judge quality. It accepts the terrible alongside the transcendent—the false starts, the to-do lists, the 3 a.m. anxieties that look absurd in daylight. And this is precisely its gift. By preserving even the mundane, it lets you trace your own becoming. You can flip back three years and find yourself worried about something long resolved, or discover an abandoned idea that suddenly, strangely, fits your present life.

Maybe that's the real point. Writing things down isn't about creating a record for history. It's a conversation with a future stranger who happens to be you—someone who will read your messy handwriting and think, *oh yes, I remember being this person*, and feel a little less alone in time.
